speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED AT FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the question asked yesterday by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition I promised I would make a statement on motions in respect of the forthcoming Commonwealth prime ministers' conference. The situation in Canada at the moment happily is such that I expect to be able to leave Ottawa tomorrow to attend the conference in London.
At that conference all but one of the members of the Commonwealth will be represented. There are now, I believe, 23 members of the Commonwealth. This shows how it has grown over recent years. The growth reflects the changed nature of the Commonwealth and indeed the changed nature of the world, because of these 23 members of the Commonwealth all but six are from Asia, Africa or the Caribbean area; all but Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Cyprus and Malta.
I believe there will be 12 or 13 prime ministers who will attend this conference, and in cases where prime ministers are unable to attend, as unfortunately is the case in respect of some members of the Commonwealth, those countries will be represented generally by their foreign or other ministers.
This will be the first meeting of the prime ministers at which a Commonwealth secretariat will be entirely in charge of the arrangements. The secretary general of the Commonwealth secretariat, a distinguished former official of the Department of External Affairs, will be the secretary general of the conference.
Undoubtedly there will be a wide range of subjects discussed. Over the years it has been the custom not to indicate in advance by means of an agenda what those subjects will be. This is a tradition which to me does not seem to have very much meaning in the present circumstances, but is one which always has been followed. So when there is a
discussion of the Commonwealth meeting in advance it is customary to say: "the following subjects likely will be discussed although no agenda has been agreed upon."
I do not think I would be betraying any secret if I were to mention two or three of the things which undoubtedly will be considered.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
The international picture generally is reviewed by the Commonwealth prime ministers, and on this occasion I am quite certain that the review will include consideration of the Viet Nam situation. It will be remembered that at the last meeting of the Commonwealth prime ministers in London over a year ago the prime ministers had a very active and, I think, valuable discussion about the Viet Nam situation, as a result of which a mission of four Commonwealth prime ministers was established and charged, if the parties to the conflict agreed, to do what they could to intervene in and mediate that situation.
It is perhaps not remembered as it should be that this mission-and three of the four members were heads of government from countries uncommitted in any way-was accepted for a visit by the governments of South Viet Nam and the United States, both of which were directly concerned, but that mission was completely rejected by the government of North Viet Nam, which made it quite clear it would not receive it in any way, shape or form. In any event, this situation will be considered again, I am sure.
There will also be a review of the disarmament position and I would expect, with particular reference to steps that have been or should be taken to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons. There will be very little at this conference in the way of economic and financial discussions; not that they are unimportant because, of course, they are, but it is extremely difficult to separate the problems in this field inside the Commonwealth association from those problems which are of world wide significance.
As I indicated the other day, there will be a meeting of the International Monetary Fund in September, at which time these matters will be discussed. Perhaps I should also have mentioned the other day that there

Commonwealth Relations will be a meeting of the Commonwealth ministers of finance in Montreal beginning September 21, at which time they will review the matters which will later come before the International Monetary Fund.
I am quite certain that the most important and the most difficult question to come before the Commonwealth prime ministers will be that of Rhodesia. It is because of that question I have said, and I do not think this is an exaggeration, that the future of the Commonwealth as a multiracial association-and that is the only basis on which it has a future-will be at stake at this meeting. In that sense the meeting will be crucial to the evolution or, indeed, the devolution of the Commonwealth of nations.
There are very deep differences of opinion in regard to the Rhodesian situation and what should be done to ensure that the illegal regime in authority there ceases to exercise that authority. These deep differences of opinion can and I think will be discussed in London in the traditional Commonwealth conference manner of complete frankness and understanding. I hope this discussion will result in some progress toward a solution to this very difficult question. We will certainly need at this conference all those qualities of frankness and freedom of discussion, and a feeling that there can be that kind of discussion conducted in mutual respect and without danger of violent misunderstanding.
So far as our own attitude is concerned, it would, of course, not be wise or prudent for me, before the conference, to indicate in detail what will be the policy of the Canadian delegation in respect of the detailed matters as they arise. It is certainly not wise to take firm and public positions on specific issues before a conference of this kind actually meets. Our basic policy in regard to Rhodesia has been made known. There have been discussions in the House of Commons, questions have been asked and answered from time to time, and there was a very good discussion of the matter before the committee on external affairs. Indeed, if it would help in any way I have no doubt that these discussions could all be put together and a memorandum or some kind of white paper issued with regard to them.
From the beginning this government, I think with the approval of all members of the house, has co-operated fully in regard to the imposition of sanctions against the illegal regime in Rhodesia. We have taken part in economic pressures which it was hoped would


bring to an end the illegal regime in that country and restore constitutional government to Rhodesia, as a first step to eventual independence on the basis of majority rule, which is the only basis on which independence can be established and accepted.

speechtext:
We have also co-operated as a government, I believe with the support of parliament, in carrying out resolutions of the United Nations security council and in carrying out the agreements of the prime ministers' conferences. We have not questioned, nor do we question now, the decision of the British government, which still has the ultimate constitutional responsibility for that country, not to use military or armed force against Rhodesia unless, as the Prime Minister of Great Britain said, such force was necessary to restore law and order. I have no doubt this matter will be re-examined at the forthcoming conference. We will certainly examine also the working of sanctions. For that purpose we will have a very detailed report from the sanctions committee which was set up after the conference of last January in Nigeria and is presided over by the Canadian high commissioner in London. We will be examining this report to see how and whether sanctions could be strengthened.
There is no doubt that the operation of sanctions as a method of bringing the regime to an end has been disappointing and that disappointment, I am sure, will be expressed in the reports we will receive. There is no doubt also that sanctions are having an effect on the economy of Rhodesia. In my own view there are still further steps that could be taken to strengthen economic pressures through sanctions. I have no doubt that proposals will be made to this end, and that one of these will be to refer the matter to the United Nations so that United Nations mandatory sanctions could be applied, either full or limited mandatory sanctions, under chapter 7 of the United Nations charter.
Under that chapter provision is made for the application of economic sanctions and military sanctions. I have always taken the stand, and I am sure hon. members agree with this, that imposing military sanctions under chapter 7 of the charter of the United Nations or under resolutions of the general assembly does not imply the use of force in the conventional sense. Nevertheless I am certain that before any use of force was contemplated under chapter 7 of the charter

there would be a full examination of whether economic sanctions under the United Nations could be applied and made effective. All these matters will be discussed and I have no idea what the results of these discussions will be. [DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
There is a very special problem with which we and other members of the Commonwealth are concerned, namely the relationship of Zambia in this situation. Zambia, which unfortunately will not be represented by its president, Kenneth Kaunda, who is one of the wise and moderating influences in African development and who will be represented by his foreign minister, is in the unenviable position of being as anxious as any country could be to see the illegal regime in Rhodesia brought to an end and replaced by one where the majority will prevail. However, at the same time Zambia is very dependent at the present time upon Rhodesia for its economic existence. If Zambia is to release itself from that dependence it is going to need economic and financial assistance from its friends in the Commonwealth and, I would hope, from outside the Commonwealth. For instance, it is an anomalous and ironic situation that one third of Rhodesian exports go to Zambia, yet Zambia is not in a position at the present time to cut off that one third which would inflict real economic damage on Rhodesia because it would destroy itself economically in the process.
This is the problem that has been actively considered in recent weeks, and proposals for assistance to Zambia by the United Kingdom and by other members of the Commonwealth including Canada will undoubtedly be considered at the conference.
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I cannot go into further details at the present time, but that is a summary of the situation which I think will confront us at the meeting which will open in London at the beginning of next week. I can only hope that out of this meeting will come some agreement which will help to solve the problems we will be facing, especially the problem of Rhodesia, the difficulty and complexity of which is greater than that which has faced, I think, any meeting of Commonwealth prime ministers.
On our ability to find some satisfactory solution to that problem, or some satisfactory progress to a solution, I think, might well depend the existence of the Commonwealth of Nations which we now know as a multiracial institution spanning the continents
Commonwealth Relations and including people of all races, of all colours and all creeds on the basis of complete equality.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED AT FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the meetings of the prime ministers of the Commonwealth are of great importance for the Commonwealth and for the peace of the world. I am happy to hear the Prime Minister's reference to the multiracial nature of the Commonwealth as being of paramount significance.
I recall the criticism in 1960 and 1961 when I took the stand-the only white prime minister to do so-that without the principle that the Commonwealth must be colour blind it could not survive. I have not changed that view. What was heresy then is now accepted.
The fact that the Prime Minister will be able to attend the conference is naturally a matter of personal pleasure. I suggested that he should do so. I brought the matter before the house, because I think it is imperative that he be there.
A prime minister's conference without prime ministers is not effective, and one of my regrets, based on the information which appeared in the press, is that the prime minister of India will not be there nor will the president of Pakistan. These are the highest representatives of areas inhabited by approximately three quarters of the population of the Commonwealth. Therefore, authoritative representations by those countries will be lacking. No one except the leaders of countries can speak for them with the authority that is necessary.
With regard to the second portion of the Prime Minister's remarks dealing with the meeting itself, I am of the opinion-and there can be disagreement with this-that it is not necessary to have a prime ministers' conference at this time. Three of them will have been called in one year. The first was in January in Africa, the second for June, and another now.
As the Prime Minister stated, the problem of Rhodesia is the one above all others that will be receiving attention. Naturally there will be a review of the world situation. The question of disarmament will receive its regular and unfinalistic review. However, the major problem is Rhodesia.
[DOT] (11:30 a.m.)
We in this party have taken the stand that Rhodesia is a matter for the United Kingdom and the responsibility of the United Kingdom. The particular relationship of Rhodesia to the

Commonwealth Relations United Kingdom places that problem in that category. I am not saying what happens there does not have an effect elsewhere in the world on the relationship between the whites and the blacks. However, the problem of Rhodesia cannot be solved by the United Kingdom placing it before a prime ministers' conference. I was strongly criticized, as were the hon. members for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), when we contended that the policy of sanctions would not work. It does not require a report by a committee of the Commonwealth nations for it to be known that sanctions have not worked. They have had their effect; they have interfered with various areas and sectors of the economy, but they just have not worked. Sanctions, on the basis of history, will not work.
Yet, one member of the government after the other, including the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), as far back as June last claimed they were working effectively. Well this is not the first time that predictions of that kind have not been borne out by events. It is generally admitted now that they have not worked. It is admitted by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, by Sir Edgar Whitehead in a recent article and by one of the great Commonwealth leaders Sir Roy Welensky. It is attested by the fact that the Smith regime is carrying on with no discernible discomfort and that Zambia will continue to be dependent on Rhodesia for oil. They have not worked. Naturally the British government wants a Commonwealth conference. This is the problem of the Wilson government, which said that it had the answers to this question.
I want to emphasize that this is not our problem. Mr. Wilson said that his solution would work. Now apparently the responsibility is again to be dissembled among the Commonwealth nations. Three meetings in one year are at least one too many. It does not make for unity to meet together regularly and not have anything particularly in mind; and there is nothing in mind on this problem except, as the Prime Minister has said, that the matter might be brought before the United Nations, and I will refer to that in a moment.
The Prime Minister mentioned, and properly, the tremendous growth of the Commonwealth with, I think he said, 23 members now. What is going to happen there? I have expressed this fear before. Today the Prime Minister speaks almost lugubriously of the

prospects for the Commonwealth. Months ago and prior to June my concern, as I expressed it, was that if a vote should take place at the prime ministers' conference, with the overwhelming number of the members of the Commonwealth of other than the white race, and that vote should be unacceptable t o Canada, or Australia, or New Zealand, or the United Kingdom, then you have the beginning of the disintegration of the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth is an amazing institution. It has no rules, no regulations, no agreement; no decisions are made, yet it has worked. I share the Prime Minister's fear that this meeting will bring about a situation that will lead to the most frightening results not in the years ahead but in the months ahead. It is because of this that I have so strongly pressed that the conference ought not to meet at this time. Time to cool has its benefits.
I know that in the last few days events have occurred that are bound to cause concern. It was only a few moments before I came into the house that I realized that this matter was going to be discussed; therefore I have before me only a few references. In the last few days Mr. Smith has acted in a way that would indicate that he is trying to meet in anticipation any action on the part of the prime ministers' conference. Up to the present Prime Minister Wilson has been talking about talks about talks. This pretty well ended in the last few days. The talks have halted, but to all intents and purposes they ended on August 25, when a bill was introduced in the Rhodesian parliament which was disastrous to the negotiations. This was a deliberate and contemptuous act designed to indicate in advance to the Commonwealth prime ministers' conference the contempt which Mr. Smith and those associated with him have for the Commonwealth.
What are the prime ministers going to do? Are they going to send the issue to the United Nations? If the matter is placed before the United Nations, what will

Are we going to have the United Nations determining the rights of individuals and the authority of a de facto government of a country which is not a member of that institution? The responsibility here rests firmly on the parliament of the United Kingdom. I repeat that Prime Minister Wilson said only a few months ago that he had the magic solution to this problem.
The Prime Minister now says, let me repeat, that the matter should be put before the United Nations. Well, as far back as January 11 or 12 of 1966 he stated that if it was not clear within a matter of weeks rather than months that existing sanctions were ending the rebellion, then further measures would have to be considered, including action in the United Nations under chapter 7. He referred to "a few weeks"; it is now months.
Chapter 7 implies military action in part. It is easy to talk of that. The Prime Minister brushed it aside, and I agree with his view. Canada should have no place whatever in any military actions that may be determined upon in this connection against a country within the Commonwealth; and no Canadian forces should be used, whether under the United Nations or otherwise, for that purpose.

We are in Cyprus as a self-appointed international policeman, at our own expense and we shall continue to pay. When I look at unification and integration and the mess they are in I can only conclude that we have come to a point in Canada where Canada's defence is to be forgotten, and in place of it involvement in international forces will be the rule. I am not going to deal with that now but I hope very shortly to do so. I can make some quotations from the texts of the minister of defence.
Having said that, I say to the Prime Minister that we can only hope this meeting will be productive of something positive regarding the Rhodesian problem. I do not know what it will be. -the embargo is being enforced: the embargo is successful.

Will the United Kingdom be willing to agree to sanctions, harsh sanctions, against not only Rhodesia but other countries such as Portugal and South Africa? Because unless that is done the sanctions cannot work; and if it is done, and Britain accepts the views of the United Nations on these things and says "We have got to clamp down on this; the sanctions must be made to work," the British crown and trade will suffer seriously and the depreciation is bound to be great, so that any question of submitting these matters to the United Nations is not very hopeful.
Indeed, that has been tried. It was tried back in May. The African nations called for the use of force in Rhodesia, I think on May 23 last, and they came before the security council. Six of the council's 15 members voted for the resolution. Among the Commonwealth there were Nigeria and Uganda. But the United States, Britain, the Netherlands, France, China, Japan, the Argentine and Uruguay abstained, with New Zealand voting against, so there is little hope that action will be taken if this matter goes to the United Nations. It is easier to state the problem than to be able to come up with any solution.
What is happening in Africa is that there is a rush toward democratic institutions and freedom without the knowledge of the operating techniques of freedom. All those countries that have rushed in to attain freedom find themselves in a serious situation. When the Prime Minister was in Nigeria, at the conference in January, he was greeted by Sir Abubakar, one of the great democratic leaders in an emerging nation, a man for whom I developed tremendous respect. A few days later he was destroyed.
What is to be done? Is it possible that the government of Canada might consider sending representatives to Rhodesia, to meet there with the representatives of the Smith administration to try and bring about something? The British cannot do it; they have shown that. The other night on television a young man with the solution for all the problems of mankind stated that Canada enjoys a high prestige in Africa. I believe that. When we were in office we were able to provide assistance to those new countries which had broken away from France and become established because of our peculiar position here in Canada. We did that, and

Would it not be a good idea if the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs were to go and try at first hand to do that which has not been achieved by the British government, which is naturally an interested party in any decisions taken, so through the medium of Canada there might be brought about some relationship which will ultimately lead to that which we all desire, namely peace with equity, and peace with the recognition that whatever the colour of a man's skin, men are equal and their rights must be respected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the prime ministers' conference which is to begin early next week meets against a background which is gloomy and foreboding. One has only to read the letter which Secretary General U Thant wrote to the security council announcing that he will not be available for another term to realize just how serious the world situation is. I think every member of parliament ought to read that letter, to see in it the despair of a man who is probably more intimately associated with the forces at work in the world today than any other human being. He cites the lack of financial support for the United Nations. He cites the war in Viet Nam as an action which in his opinion, if not stopped, could ultimately lead to a major catastrophe.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
Therefore it seems to me that the Commonwealth prime ministers are meeting at a most appropriate time. The right hon. Prime Minister said that two subjects would be discussed, one being the question of Viet Nam. I think it is a matter of regret that the Commonwealth prime ministers' delegation which endeavoured to meet with the various parties in the Viet Nam dispute was rejected by some of the disputants. This is a view which I expressed as forcefully as I could when our parliamentary delegation met Mr. Mikoyan, who at that time was President of the U.S.S.R. However, I hope the prime ministers' conference will not allow this rejection to dissuade them from whatever other action they can take.
One of the hopeful signs is that Canada and India, two of the members of the Commonwealth, are two of the members on the international control commission. If it is not
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

possible to get the two co-chairmen of the Geneva accord powers to reconvene that conference, I think Canada and India might well discuss the possibility of themselves calling a conference and inviting all those who are affected, including the national liberation front in South Viet Nam.
It may be that Peking and Hanoi would refuse to attend, although I seriously doubt it.
I doubt if they could stay away from a conference called by two members of the international control commission, two countries which have nothing to gain by prolonging the war in Viet Nam.
I hope the Prime Minister will use all the influence he can to persuade the Commonwealth Prime Ministers to speak out on the question of Viet Nam, and to urge the Commonwealth at least to endorse publicly the basic proposals put forth by U Thant, the secretary general of the United Nations, for a cessation of the bombing, for a conference of all groups including the national liberation front, for the eventual withdrawal of all foreign troops, and for the right of the people in Viet Nam to determine in free elections what form of government they wish to have.
The second question the Prime Minister said will be discussed is Rhodesia. I cannot agree with the right hon. Leader of the Opposition that this conference should not be held at this time. I think it is imperative that the conference should be held at this time. It is true that constitutionally this problem is the responsibility of Great Britain, but if all the members of the Commonwealth, including Canada, do nothing; if there is no attempt to find a solution, what will inevitably happen is that members of the Commonwealth in Africa and even in Asia may one by one withdraw from the Commonwealth.
We can destroy the Commonwealth by inaction. We cannot do any harm by having the prime ministers meet. While it may be Great Britain's responsibility even the British government, or any other government, is surely not averse to getting the consensus of other nations which are equally concerned about preserving the Commonwealth as a force in the world. I think this is the time for the prime ministers of the Commonwealth to meet.
It is true that there is no easy solution, but it seems to me there are three courses of action open. The first is to do nothing and to allow matters to go on just as they are. Apparently the economic sanctions have not been
September 2, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES	8013
completely effective, although undoubtedly they have had some effect. But if nothing is done there will undoubtedly be a withdrawal of some of the African Commonwealth countries from this association, and that could even be followed by the withdrawal of some of the Asiatic members from the Commonwealth.
If Mr. Ian Smith and his illegal regime carry out their threat of revising the constitution so that Mr. Smith can jail his opponents without trial, there could be bloodshed in Africa; there could be intervention by other African countries; there could be the beginning of a war between Africans and whites that would shake that whole unhappy continent. It seems to me that to take the policy of despair and say there is nothing we can do, and just let events take their course, is a complete abdication of statesmanship.
With respect to the other alternative that has been mentioned, of military sanctions against Rhodesia, apart from the moral consideration it is doubtful if Great Britain could assemble a military force and launch a military attack against a country as isolated as Rhodesia. There is another consideration apart from the military logistics. It is that a war between the forces of Great Britain or the Commonwealth and the illegal regime of Mr. Ian Smith might be an invitation to the 4 million blacks in that country to rise, and an invitation to other African countries to intervene.
It seems to me that the only solution which appears to be in sight at the moment, unless the prime ministers when they meet next week find some better proposal, is to submit this matter to the United Nations and ask the United Nations to impose mandatory economic sanctions. I recognize all that has been said about what this would entail. It may mean not only economic sanctions against Rhodesia but may mean economic sanctions against Portugal and South Africa. I recognize that Great Britain is very dependent at the present time upon its trade relations with South Africa, and that the imposition of mandatory economic sanctions by the United Nations under its charter would involve very considerable financial sacrifices for the United Kingdom.
But, Mr. Speaker, peace, like everything else, has a price. We have to decide whether we are prepared to pay the price to maintain a world in which the rule of law obtains. We must decide whether we are going to see a
Commonwealth Relations police state with a racist government continue a policy which could lead to a conflagration in Africa, or whether the United Nations will take whatever steps are necessary to guarantee the freedom of over 4 million Africans who at the present time are living under a totalitarian regime imposed upon them by less than a quarter of a million white supremacists.
I think Canada has to give its support to any such proposal if the Commonwealth is prepared to make an advance to the United Nations. It has been asked, "What can the United Nations do"? Well, Mr. Speaker, if we adopt a policy of despair that the United Nations can do nothing, and if this body, which was launched with such hope and optimism in 1945, is now so completely decrepit and useless that we cannot refer this matter to it, the future is filled with impending gloom.
[DOT] (12 noon)
I for one do not regret that Canada has contributed to the maintenance of peace in Gaza, Cyprus or anywhere else. Any small price Canada has paid out of its great affluence to maintain peace in any part of the world is a small price to pay. Peace is indivisible. Wherever there is war, dissention or racial discrimination in any part of the earth the peace of the world is in danger and the freedom of mankind is at stake. If Canada, by giving its support wherever such contribution is necessary financially, whatever sacrifices are involved, can contribute to the establishment of a genuine democratic government in Rhodesia with equality of treatment for all its citizens whether black or white, that, Mr. Speaker, will be a small price to pay for reaching such a satisfactory situation. I hope the Prime Minister will use his very considerable influence at this conference, in the absence of any other course of action which with his knowledge of the facts may seem preferable, to urge that the situation not be allowed to deteriorate further and, if Great Britain does not feel it can act on its own or if the Commonwealth does not feel it has any solution at hand, to urge that this matter be taken to the United Nations with a request that they deal with this troubled spot before it spreads throughout Africa and endangers the peace of the world.
The Prime Minister of Canada goes to this conference with very considerable prestige, prestige on his own account because of his long record in international affairs and his well-known interest in the cause of peace. He

Commonwealth Relations also goes with considerable prestige because Canada is a country which has the respect and I think the affection of many of the countries of Africa and Asia. We have stood with them on many occasions not only under the present Prime Minister but also under the former prime minister. We have stood with the African and Asian people in many of their disputes with the western powers. I think Canada is respected and will be listened to.
I believe our Prime Minister probably can wield more influence in discussions with the Commonwealth leaders of Africa and Asia than can any other white leader who will be present at this conference next week. Therefore I say to the Prime Minister that he goes to this conference, I am sure, with the best wishes of the Canadian people and carries on his shoulders our hopes and aspirations. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) told us that 12 or 13 prime ministers of commonwealth nations would meet in London in a few days.
According to the Prime Minister, the international situation will be discussed during this conference. It is perfectly normal that prime ministers of commonwealth nations deal with the international situation and they will naturally discuss the American escalation in Viet Nam.
But I do not see how the commonwealth prime ministers could decide anything about Viet Nam. Since Canada is geographically located next to the most powerful country in the world, in the past the American government and the Canadian government have discussed the Viet Nam issue and will continue to do so in the future without seeking the advice of the other prime ministers of commonwealth nations because in some cases, Canada has to take positions that other commonwealth countries do not have or do not want to take. This is quite normal, precisely because of our geographical location and the close ties between the American and the Canadian people.
Another subject that will probably be brought up is that inflation which is presently causing great damage in Great Britain and in many other countries. But it seems that the

DEBATES	September 1, 1966
most debated question will be that of Rhodesia. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister devoted two thirds of his statement to the Rhodesian problem. Before dealing with Rhodesia, the Prime Minister announced that the Ministers of Finance will meet on September 21 in Montreal to review our position with regard to the International Monetary Fund. I sincerely hope and suggest to the Prime Minister that he bring together the federal and provincial Ministers of Finance in order to review our monetary position right here without having to resort to the International Monetary Fund.
To revert to the question of Rhodesia, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said that Canada had to impose economic restrictions in the case of Rhodesia because the government there is illegal.
I am not questioning the fact that there is an illegal government in Rhodesia, but Rhodesia is not the only country with an illegal government. I suspect that in Russia, the government there is not quite legal. I do not think that in China, the government is quite legal either. In Cuba, the government is not quite legal. In other countries of the world there are governments that are not quite legal, but this does not prevent us from dealing with them, from making large deals with them.
Now, as for Rhodesia, we must be concerned directly in its situation, or rather in the position they are taking.
This should not be taken to mean that I approve what the present illegal government of Rhodesia is doing in that country, far from it, but I am in full agreement with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he says, for instance, that the problem of Rhodesia is no concern of Canada, it is the concern of Britain. This is true. This concerns the Wilson government, in Britain.
It does not concern us here. There have been skirmishes between Britain and Rhodesia, but that is no concern of ours. We have nothing to do with that and the Leader of the Opposition is right on that score. I understand the problem is most delicate and that every means are being sought to sanction and strangle Rhodesia and incite the people of Rhodesia to throw out a government which is considered illegal.
The people, men, women, and children suffer from these economic sanctions pressed upon them, because an illegal government is

in power, like so many others all over the world.
Mr. Speaker, the problem is delicate and the right hon. It cannot do without Rhodesia. Canada could grant Zambia massive exports in order to substitute for Rhodesia.
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel these considerations contribute to the settlement of the Rhodesian question. Neither do I believe that Canada should be very much involved in the affair. I do not feel it should be. And for these reasons, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition is right in saying that the Rhodesian question concerns the Wilson government in Great Britain. He is right.

I know how strongly the right hon. Prime Minister feels about world peace and good feelings throughout the world. I am aware of the fact that he was with the Department of External Affairs for many years and that he is thoroughly competent in this field. I know that the right hon. Prime Minister will enjoy, at this conference, great prestige, but is it not a fact that, on that occasion, Canada's influence, the Prime Minister's influence, is due to our being neighbours of the United States and that country is known as the most powerful in the world? That is reflected upon us Canadians, members of the government or of the Canadian parliament.
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister enjoys this influence, to be sure, but let us use it to promote amity, cordiality, understanding, co-operation between nations. I am sure that the Prime Minister will measure up to expectations at this conference of prime ministers of Commonwealth countries, and my best wishes go with him. I am of the opinion that Canada stands to gain therefrom and I hope that the Prime Minister sees to it that the word "peace" is not merely an expression to be used right and left, without ever knowing where it should be applied. May it be used everywhere, in Rhodesia as

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that with all of the concern and advice expressed to the right hon. Prime Minister he will not have very much difficulty at the conference of prime ministers next week. I suppose there may be some disagreement on the part of the prime ministers of Australia and New Zealand, so far as the advice given about Viet Nam by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) is concerned, in view of their stake in the southeast Asia situation. I can imagine as well that it will be difficult to get agreement among the leaders of the governments of the African Commonwealth countries.
It is with sorrow and a heavy heart that we look back at the last eight months and realize that a number of the men who would normally have been representatives of countries such as Nigeria are no longer alive as a result of two military coups that have taken place. Likew.se there has been an upheaval in Ghana. The whole situation as to alignment or non-alignment with the great powers of the world is certainly not as fixed as it was a year ago.
I am sure the Prime Minister will be a little confused as a result of some of the remarks of the Leader of the Official Opposition who talked about three Commonwealth prime ministers' conferences held this year. If my memory serves me right, this is merely the second conference. The July conference that was to follow the January conference held in Lagos was postponed because of disagreement and lack of clarity so far as the problems in Rhodesia were concerned, so really this is the second conference of the Commonwealth prime ministers to be held this year rather than the third. Whether it is the third or second conference, Mr. Speaker, the grim realities of the world situation faced by the commonwealth prime ministers are something that do not give reason for very much cheer or optimism so far as the future of the world is concerned.

Commonwealth Relations
I only wish to say to the Prime Minister at this time that the most important thing in the Commonwealth and in the world is reasonable judgment and understanding by literate men of good will. There is no magic formula that will solve the problems of Rhodesia and Viet Nam. There is no easy way out of these problems. What we need in the world is balance, and that can only come from men of good judgment and understanding who fully appreciate the problems and what is at stake.
When we consider the situation in Africa and realize how interdependent these countries are so far as their economies are concerned, when we look at the history of the world during the last few years, and listen to the cries of uhuru and peace, when we consider the responsibilities of governments and administrations that must make decisions, it is easy to understand why this conference will not be an easy one. It will be difficult for the Prime Minister in his particular position as leader of a country which is respected, and for which there is great affection to give leadership during the deliberations that will take place and at the same time give consideration to every country's problems.
The fact that Zambia is as dependent as she is upon Rhodesia and Rhodesia upon Zambia and the fact that colour of skin and racial problems are not solved just by the declaration of high sounding principles point to the soberness and importance of this conference. These facts also point to the need for getting together and talking things over on a reasonable basis. If that requires another conference this year at which this kind of discussion can take place, then let us have another one, because as long as people are talking and trying to understand each other there is hope that some kind of satisfactory arrangement can be made.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, let me say in regard to the problems of Rhodesia that reason must be applied. The changing of so-called illegal governments by the normal process of democratic elections in countries such as Rhodesia is something that just cannot happen. There must be a period of time during which Rhodesia can be properly prepared for the processes of a true democracy, and this is something that will only result from the efforts of literate men and women who have some background in the administration of public affairs. If that can be done I am sure that Rhodesia as well as other African countries can live in harmony. In this

way I am sure that some answer can be found to the problems which relate to black and white, underdeveloped, senior and junior Commonwealth countries and, indeed, perhaps even to the Viet Nam situation.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, personally and on behalf of our party I wish the Prime Minister and his staff well in the deliberations they face. I say again that we understand the importance of this meeting and the tremendous weight of the problems to be faced. We trust that, as has been characteristic of Commonwealth prime ministers and Commonwealth countries, men coming together to talk over their problems will be able to come to some reasonable solution and that step by step men and nations will be led forward in order that we may obtain the proper and full development of our resources both material and human.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, September 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pickersgill for the second reading of Bill No.
Transportation
C-231, to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night in my remarks on second reading of this bill, because of the possibility that we would be called to the other place I had time to make only one or two general observations in an effort to highlight what I think is the significance of the big change in the situation now from what it was at the time of the MacPherson report. Today I should like to develop my thoughts in a more sedate and orderly manner than was possible last night. In 1964 when the resolution in respect of Bill C-120 was on the order paper I had a discussion with various members of the government at which time it was intimated that the bill which was being introduced at that time was the bill of the previous government with some improvement. I spoke on behalf of the opposition and indicated general support of those principles. At that time I warned that when the bill was presented to us we would be very wary of it, but outside of that I think it can be said that generally I gave approval to the idea that now is the time to take a big new look at the whole question of railway legislation in this country.
In my speech on that occasion I outlined the history of railway development in Canada. I pointed out how in the course of time the application of flat freight rate increases across the country had affected the prairie areas and the maritimes. It was this unjust discrimination in rates that caused so much dissension in our country for so long, and as a government we were determined to halt it. We set up the royal commission on transportation in 1959. The fundamental job of this commission was to examine the whole railway structure in Canada in the light of the present development of our country in an effort to lay down ground rules so that the railways could operate efficiently in Canada and at the same time end this discrimination in respect of rates in various regions.
Those were the fundamental purposes of the royal commission on transportation headed eventually by Mr. MacPherson. In 1964 we were beginning to feel that the recommendations of the MacPherson report had to be modified because of the fact that they left up in the air any practical way of achieving the

September 2, 1966
Transportation
objectives of that report. In 1964 our attention was concentrated on the question of rationalization of railway management and operation primarily in the prairies where the greatest problems lay.
When the bill was produced in 1964 it was immediately very clear that the ideas we on this side of the house had were not being implemented. We had felt that if there was some way of getting the two major railways in western Canada to rationalize their efforts, then not only would there be more efficient railway transportation in the prairies but also the necessity of always claiming there were losses on the Crowsnest pass rates would end.
One of the greatest myths ever promulgated in this country is that the railway shippers in Canada are asked to subsidize the movement of western grain into world markets. This myth was finally destroyed last night when the minister accepted the proposition of no losses and said that is why they took the subsidies out of the bill. So at this moment I am speaking to those in central Canada who have lived comfortably all these years with the myth that they were subsidizing the movement of western grain into world markets. This has now been exposed as a myth. This is one of the points I wished to make.
In so far as the rationalization provisions of the 1964 bill are concerned, they failed because of a very simple fact. A rationalization board was set up and at the time the rationalization board was given no power to deal with anything. Therefore we had to point out that this was a complete farce from the point of view of trying to fool the people into believing that there was going to be a rational operation of our railways in western Canada.
Recommendations for the improvement of railway operations in western Canada have been made for over 30 years. Very few of these recommendations have been accepted. Many of us have come to the conclusion that until there is leadership provided by the government or parliament in directing the railways of this country, particularly in western Canada, to run on a rational basis they will not be run on that basis but will continue the inefficient practices that have been developed.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
No one wants to go back and rehash the history of the railway companies in western Canada. Suffice it to say that the Canadian Pacific Railway, which first entered that area, over the years has developed what could be IMr. Hamilton.]
described as a reasonably efficient and integrated system. As a result of the enthusiasm on the part of the railway companies at the turn of the century and the ability of the prairie provinces to produce agricultural products they built railway lines all over the country. That is what precipitated the railway building spree. Lines moved in all directions. If one company built a line it was duplicated by another company, and we have had to pay for this situation for two generations.
This is the time to end this hodgepodge railway operation in western Canada. At this time when we are considering this legislation I am sure most of us agree that we desire forward progress and an end to this hodgepodge operation. The bill presented to the house in 1964 gave no power to the rationalization board to deal with this situation. Instead of rationalization all the board did was to turn over an application for abandonment to the Board of Transport Commissioners. Then traditionally, as always has been the case, the board accepted the railway figures.
Railway operational costing is so complicated that as yet there is no accurate system acceptable to experts. We had a bill before us in 1964 which turned over the whole question of whether a line would be abandoned, and whether the government or the taxpayers would pay a subsidy to keep the line in operation, to the board of transport commissioners. This was bad legislation because it only dealt with the question whether a line from point A to point B was paying or not paying and whether it should be abandoned or subsidized by the taxpayers. That did not provide an answer.
We intended that this rationalization board should have the power to look at each area of the prairie provinces where there was a duplication of railway services, railways running parallel for miles because they did not wish to use each other's lines, and decide whether there was an anomaly. We thought this board had the power to direct the railway companies to run these lines efficiently and within limits of ordinary common sense. We were convinced that once this took place there would be no railway line in western Canada that was not running at a profit.
In my speech in 1964 I made the proposal, even before I saw the bill, that we should divide western Canada into areas. The bill before us has accepted that principle. Since the bill of 1964 was presented our knowledge
September 2, 1966

has increased and the principles envisaged at that time are no longer the right ones. The concept of the bill now before us incorporates a better idea so far as lines in western Canada are concerned.
We are now aware that most of the railway lines in western Canada are not only economical but produce a profit because of the tremendous increase in transported goods in the last two years. That does not necessarily mean that the railways are now making money. Let us not allow these anomalies to continue because of the operation of unnecessary lines. We could reduce costs even more than they have been reduced in recent years and effect greater profits.
Last night I said I hoped the railways would use the potential increase in profits to purchase new equipment and to make railway employees' wages equivalent to those being paid in similar types of industry. For generations we have asked railway employees in this country to refrain from seeking to have their wages grow in pace with the country's wealth and in pace with other sections of the economy. During the last few years we thought the railway industry was dying.
The third general suggestion I made last night was that we expect the railways to make this major change in thinking as a result of which not only will higher profits result but better wages, better equipment and lower freight rates. When the railways eventually adopt the concept of expansion it will follow in a rational way that rates can be reduced, resulting in more business.
Having reviewed railway history in a minor way let me now indicate that during past debates and discussions of this situation I have tried to be helpful. This is the time we should think in terms of action based on straight thinking. Let me put on record some ideas which I think will help this house to think along these lines.
Bill C-231 is a much improved bill compared with Bill C-120 presented to the house in 1964. The minister deserves congratulations because he has tried to understand this very complex situation and has put into this bill wording which indicates that new concepts are developing. This is indicated by the measure now before us.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I must be honest and say I do not think it will help management, labour or shippers unless we propose ideas during this debate or at the
Transportation
committee stage which are practical and helpful. Before I attempt to do so let me remind the minister of what I said briefly last night. One or two principles embodied in this measure terrify me. The first relates to freight rates, and I will deal with that subject in greater detail in a moment or two.
A very real difference is developing in thinking regarding rationalization in order to remove the fear of western Canada about line abandonment. I am sure the minister knows the situation I have in mind. What are the new facts regarding this new concept? Railways are not declining as a mode of transport any longer. The change began in 1961. The one thing more than anything else which reversed that thought was the commencement of grain sales to China and other eastern European countries. Railways are no longer declining as an efficient method of transportation. It took some time after 1961 for us to realize that changes were taking place. Let me list some of the changes that have occurred.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I quoted these figures in a hurry last night and I should like to re-emphasize them. Using round figures, though I am sure the experts will not quarrel with them, as late as 1958 approximately 400 million bushels of grain were moved out of western positions. In the crop year just completed over 800 million bushels of grain were moved. The significance of these figures when applied to railway hauling can only be understood if one recognizes that the greatest part of the cost of running a railway is fixed. It does not make any difference whether no trains run or a great many trains run; there are certain fixed costs.
In my early days of studying railway economics we used to use the rough figure of 60 per cent or 70 per cent as representing the fixed costs of a railway operation. I have no recent figures but I hope to get them. If 70 per cent of the costs are fixed and you suddenly double the tonnage of goods being moved on the railway, the proportion of fixed costs drops away down and your profits rise tremendously. This can be demonstrated most dramatically in charts to show what happens to the cost per unit of freight hauled.
The movement of grain is in itself only a single fact in the new situation, but being such a large bulk product it is a very important part of our economy. Just a few years ago we in some parts of western Canada used to generate 20,000 or 25,000 bushels of grain

September 2, 1966
Transportation
per mile. Now in these same areas it is over
80,000	bushels per mile. A revolution has taken place in respect of this one item. Because of these facts we must make sure that in the parliament of our country we legislate on the basis of a growing, expanding industry and do not legislate to share the poverty of a dying industry.
The second point I want to make concerns the huge increase in goods that flow back from the central provinces into the prairies. This development has occurred in the last five or six years. We must recognize the tremendous number of dollars of new earning power that has poured into the prairies since 1961, first of all from the sale of the great quantities of unused and unsold grain and, second from the tremendous crops we grew in 1962, 1963, 1964, 1965 and, I trust, with God's help in this year 1966. These tremendous sales of grain and increased income have meant that a tremendous increase in purchasing power has poured into the central provinces and British Columbia. As a consequence our trains are carrying a tremendous back-haul of goods from the central areas of our country into the prairies. The importance of this situation is that when the railways are hauling goods both ways the amount of profit rises in a general ratio rather than in a direct line proportion. I wish I had the time and statistical staff to put before the house the extent to which this back-haul has grown in the last five years.
Third, Mr. Speaker, on the point that the railways are not a declining mode of transport I would refer also to potash, a new product. Potash is one of the three main fertilizers needed to keep our land productive in order to feed the people of the world. Potash is not needed for Canadian soils at the present time, at least, not in western Canada because our soils are too new and it will probably be a century before we have to use potash in order to restore the fertility of that land. But the great continents of the world, Asia, for example, where civilization has existed for 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 years, need this product. The old continent of Africa needs it as do the newer areas of civilization in western Europe. South American and other areas with teeming millions are not as productive on the land as they should be and there is an increasing need for potash.
These vast areas of the world need the potash that is buried under the soil of the province of Saskatchewan and to some extent in Alberta and Manitoba. At the present time

our production of potash is approximately 2 million tons a year but by 1970, with markets that are already known, the need for potash exports out of the west coast will be at least 4 million tons, and certainly between 1970 and 1975 the export of potash from the prairies to the west coast alone will have reached 7 million tons. This is on the basis of known markets, and the figures I have quoted do not include any figure for China where 700 million people now live. By 1980 the population of China will be 1 billion people. In the south of that country they grow three crops a year. One crop has to be wasted in growing grain fertilizer in the form of clover. In the north of that country they grow two crops a year, one of which is used for fertilizer. Chemical fertilizing alone will increase production in southern China by a third and in northern China by half. Here we have a market in addition to the markets I have already indicated. This will demonstrate to the house the tremendous movement of bulk products in Canada to our coasts.
I am sorry I do not have any estimates for the movement of this product to the south, the eastern markets and the markets of Europe and Africa. I am only positive of one thing, that they will be there, and I am sure that unless we learn new techniques in the next few years, for a good while at least these products will be carried by rail cars. I know of the work being done in connection with pipe lines. However, in potash alone the demand is tremendous. The only way I can explain this sensibly and make it understandable is by comparing it with a product we all know, namely, wheat. Those who have seen the hundreds of railway trains carrying our wheat to market will realize that an equal number of trains will be required to carry potash and they will have an idea of the expansion that will take place in western Canada in this connection.
I have dealt with potash, Mr. Speaker, but I do not want to overlook the fact that products like sulphur, a by-product of our oil and gas wells, are now in great demand all over the world. I believe that just a year ago one million tons of sulphur went through the port of Vancouver. I would suggest that in this item alone there will be a tremendous tonnage in the future. We know that Japan wants our coal and that Japan and other nations want many of our mineral ores in concentrated form. We know there is a great demand in many parts of the world for our
l.p.p. fuels, butane, propane, methane and so
September 2, 1966

on. Although many of these fuels are carried in pipe lines, a great quantity is still carried by rail.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
To give hon. members an illustration of the attitude on the part of railway management that we have to fight, I mention the Pine Point Railway. In 1958 the then prime minister of our country announced in Winnipeg a ten-point, over-all development program. One of these points concerned the building of a railroad to the south shore of Great Slave Lake. I well recall the laughs and mockery at that time. Some said it was a vision.
Let me relate to the house the significance of Pine Point not only to the development of new wealth in this country but to railway profits and operations. The Pine Point Railway runs for approximately 400 miles from Steen at the end of the Northern Alberta Railway.
The property at the end of the railway was owned at that time by a subsidiary of Co-minco which is in turn a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Naturally we went to the railway and asked if they would not co-operate in building this 400 miles of line to Great Slave lake in order to haul the lead and zinc from the vast volume of reserves to help us develp not only a needed resource but also to establish an economic base and platform on which we could develop the whole Mackenzie river basin. The attitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway is well known. They refused to take part in the building of this railway. As a result the C.N.R. built the line on the guarantee of the federal government and rates were set to make the hauling of the ore from Pine Point compensatory. I believe the C.N.R. got the hauling rights for that ore down to Calgary and the C.P.R. takes it over the mountains to Kimberley and Trail.
The point I am making can best be described by giving some of the rough figures which have appeared in the press regarding the value of that mine in the first year. The mine started to operate when the railway was completed in the fall of 1964. The first full year of operations was 1965 and I think the capital cost was roughly $25 million. The profits in the first year of $22 million were sufficient to pay off most of the capital costs of the mine in that one year. The year 1966 is not over and if I read the press correctly profits on the Pine Point mine this year are running at approximately $36 million.
Transportation
Here is my point, Mr. Speaker. This mine has risen in value because there was a sale for its products. Everyone was so involved with the glamour of rising stock prices that they forgot the tremendous importance to the railway economy of this movement of tonnage to the places I have named, which has made the whole fabric of railway transportation in western Canada that much stronger. It is quite clear that these mineral ores are not unimportant to the wealth of the country and to the wealth of our railways.
The second major fact I wish to emphasize is the need for more capital equipment on the railways. First of all we need more motive power to meet the expanding needs of the railways. Last year the C.P.R. leased some locomotives but now I think they should realize that what is required, with a rising demand for railway transport, is not a one-shot deal but that this demand will continue not only for transporting grain but many other commodities. We need this motive power to move a tremendous volume of goods faster and more efficiently.
We need to make use of modern technology, new grain cars and new ore cars. We still use cars with side loading for hauling grain. We started to use them in the last century and, by George, we are still using them. The building of artificial false doors, lining the cars with paper, loading the grain into the centre of the car and pushing it back require a tremendous amount of time. When the cars arrive at the terminal the same operations have to be repeated in reverse except for the fact that they have a few gadgets now to lift the grain car at each end.
I am simply suggesting that the modern type of grain car, which is open at the top, carries three times as much grain and can be dumped in a few seconds, as fast as the grain can pour out of the big opening, is one of the things that are necessary to decrease costs and increase the service to the shipper.
Another thing that we need is more new port facilities. This is in itself a whole new field. I have seen lakers on the Great Lakes carrying a million bushels of grain. They can now be unloaded in a matter of hours. Yet in some of our ports the operation takes four days. Shovels are still used to load or unload a million bushels of grain. I see in other places great boat-loading facilities and when I realize that we still continue to use the old techniques at our terminals I suggest, even though this is not dealt with in the bill, that what is needed among other things to make

September 2, 1986
Transportation
the railway system efficient is a complete revision of our port facilities. I suggest that this matter should be dealt with at an early opportunity.
To those of us who come from the prairies I say, without fear of contradiction, that we need a modernized country elevator system. We still use the same elevators that were used at the turn of the century. There is such a devotion to the old type of country elevator system in western Canada that it is hardly recognized that this method is costing the farmer 3 to 7 cents a bushel more than what he would be charged if we had a new system. This matter has a bearing on railway rationalization. Before you can ask the elevator companies to accelerate the building of a modern country elevator system you have to come up with a rational plan, not in 15 years but in the next year or so, whereby the companies can be told where these elevators can be built safely.
The third fact I want to put forward has to do with the question of rationalization which I have referred to once or twice before. I think I have made it clear that the government must lead and must act in this field. The bill says that the Commission may make recommendations to the railways. To me this is a waste of time. There is one section in the bill which can be utilized and which give the government power to clear up these points in a matter of two or three years. I say this power should be used.
Running rights are not new, and if I had to mention every single case in western Canada where foolishness in operation exists I would be here for many an hour speaking about it. Naturally one tends to pick the examples with which one is familiar, but when I think of some of the great areas of grain production in western Canada, the Goose Lake area, towns like Eatonia, Snipe Lake, Eston, Hughton, Forgan, Dinsmore and all the other grain towns through which a tremendous volume of grain passes, I do not need to be an expert in railway management to know that unnecessary cost is involved. The answer is so simple. For example, if we could get the C.N.R. to switch its trains to C.P.R. lines, go across the Outlook bridge and get back to the main line, that would be one case where a saving could be made. Rationalization was a new idea a few years ago but now it is a fact which we must accept. We can no longer let the railways dither and delay accepting efficient methods of operation. If we have to put up millions of dollars in subsidies for the

railways we do not want to see these subsidies used for inefficient operations. This is the main point I am making. This is a new factor, and we must accept this principle of rationalization.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Another factor is productivity. I do not know how many Canadians know it but in the last few years some 12 million or 13 million acres of land in western Canada have had the bush cut off, the stumps pulled up and the land broken to produce more grain. These 12 million or 13 million acres account for more good farmland than Ontario uses. This is what these so-called broken down, small bush farmers in the west have done in the last few years. It is a revolution in itself. All the economists, all the experts have been telling these smaller farmers that they are finished. They have been saying that you have to have a great, big farm. The farmers say, we homesteaded this land or our fathers or grandfathers did and we are not going to give it up. They have cleared the bush, broken this land and now they are able to produce crops quite easily so that now we have a production of 700 million bushels plus.
The point I am trying to make is that many lines that are up for abandonment are in these areas which were not heavy grain producers a few years ago. What little grain they did produce was used to feed live-stock. Now they are areas with tremendous surpluses. A few years ago when I was the minister in charge of the Wheat Board I used to think a three or four bushel quota would clean up the grain in these areas with smaller farms. We know now that these are areas with heavy surpluses of grain. Larger quotas have cleared the grain off the big farms which were supposed to be efficient. However, the little fellow is now using machinery just as the big fellow does. He is using fertilizer and he has new land. In addition, he has an incentive to produce which he did not have five or six years ago because he knows he can sell his grain.
This means we have a new factor to consider. Many of these areas were not considered to be big revenue producers for the railway but they are now large grain producing areas. This is a new situation which I have put on the record in some detail. We have to face the fact that there is a new situation. I was hoping this bill would have indicated a realization of these new factors which are not particularly secret. They are
September 2, 1966

well known. I hoped the bill would indicate a complete break with the philosophy of the past, namely, that the railways' share of the traffic was dropping from 60 per cent to 40 per cent and therefore we should ease their misery in their declining years. Instead we get a bill which, when we read the sections dealing with branch line abandonments, indicates the tortuous process we will have to go through in connection with the abandonment of lines.
If I may, I should like to take the liberty of quoting from the bill. The government is very kind to us. When lines are going to be abandoned posters are going to be put up all
over the place.

speechtext: Death by inches.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
It will be death by slow strangulation. I find one example on page 24
of the bill. It reads:
The company shall post in each station of the branch line to be abandoned under this section and keep so posted for such period as may be prescribed by the commission a notice of any order or direction under subsection (4) or (5) made in respect of that line.
If you read the other sections, you will find they are going to give us five years of living on borrowed time. I have one other example which is found on page 32. Reading this section is like drum-fire on our sensitive nerve ends. It deals with costs and claims and reads in part as follows:
(a)	post notices at stations served by the passenger train service; and
(b)	publish notices in any paper or papers circulating in the area served by the passenger-train service.
We are going to be the best informed of any people in the world as we go to the hangman's noose. I could not help but tell the minister last night that in my opinion this bill is a pessimistic one. All I have to do to give myself nightmares is to take all the applications for railway line abandonment, take a coloured pencil and put a heavy line along those lines in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. It is the most frightening map at which you can look, particularly when you estimate the number of people who are going to be affected.
Last night, therefore, I made an appeal to the minister to see to it that the situation is not hopeless. In view of the facts I have just given we should take away this fear of abandonment. We should end the long drawn out process outlined in this legislation for han-
Transportation
dling abandonments. In addition, we should increase the efficiency of railway operations so they can make more money and I hope they use some of it to pay their men additional wages and reduce freight rates.
In order to make this possible we need, in addition to what we have in the bill, more than an oral statement from the minister that his intentions are to go even farther. I should like to see a written statement from the government setting forth government policy. The branch line procedures outlined in this bill add to the fear under which we have lived for the last number of years. There are doubts about the government in western Canada. A definite and clear statement of this kind, which we knew could not be changed, would clear away one of the issues dividing us in this house. It would get these abandonments off our necks. We are going to have a big enough fight on railway freight rates without getting into a fight about railway line abandonments. I know the government has been working on this matter and I should like to get a statement of clarification so that we can vote on the other principles contained in this bill. I do not want to go into all the details but I think the minister can guess what they are.

speechtext: Rather easily.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: The first thing we need is a declaration by the government that all applications for railway line abandonment in western Canada are going to be thrown out. The next thing would be to issue a list of lines on which the government would not accept applications for abandonment until 1975 or for about ten years. From the amount of use made of lines in western Canada not only for grain but for other bulk products I know the lines that will be on this first list. They will be the majority of the lines for which applications have been received for abandonment. I ask that those lines not only be taken off the list but be protected for ten years.

Would the former minister like to ask me now?

I have one more statement to make and then I will ask the question.
The third thing I want is an undertaking in this written statement that a plan of this kind will be undertaken in the form of a consensus arrangement in the sense that we will all know now the lines that will be considered

for abandonment. Then members in this house will know how they are affected. If there is general agreement on this, then they can go forward. The ones on which there was going to be debate could go through the procedures outlined in the bill and we are prepared to accept those long procedures. Let us remove this fear of abandonment from the minds of so many thousands of our western people. My question to the minister is this. Will he consider giving an undertaking in writing to remove these applications entirely, to list the lines in relation to which no applications will be considered, and will he let us know which lines will be in doubt, so that we can begin to get down to making decisions?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member is awfully good to let me intervene at this point to answer his question, and I appreciate it very much. I saw the presidents of the railways this morning, but for another reason. I took advantage of the meeting to ask them whether I might be permitted to say that on the very day on which this legislation passed they would withdraw all their existing applications for abandonment on the prairies, and that they would revise their applications in the light of the decisions made by parliament and put forward in the legislation, not as it stands at the moment necessarily but as it emerges from the committee and is passed by parliament. I was given the authority of the presidents of the railways to say that that would be done.
In other words, all those applications which are in suspension, none of which is being proceeded with, will be withdrawn on the day the legislation is completed. I think it is only fair that they should wait until then, because they would prejudice their own position if they acted and if we did not proceed with the legislation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Would they be refiled the next day?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
They would only be filed on the basis of what parliament decided in the legislation which was passed.
To answer the hon. gentleman's second question, I thought I indicated in a general way last night-but I think I can be a little more specific in reply to his question-that I hope to get the approval of my colleagues to some of these things, though not perhaps before second reading because this week has not been an easy week to conduct deliberations with them. However, the government
[Mr. Hamilton.)
has already decided in principle that a network of railways in western Canada will be guaranteed as essential for a period of years.
Just as soon as it is possible for me to give the details I will give them to the house or to the committee and make them public. I will also give the date before which no applications under any procedures for abandonment will be considered on this essential network. As the hon. gentleman has said, I think that will accomplish the second purpose.
The inference to be drawn from this, of course, as all hon. members will realize, is that those lines which are not included in the guaranteed network will therefore be candidates for abandonment by whatever system parliament decides on. However, I think that that means that even a lot of those lines may not necessarily be abandoned. Some of them will not. However, they would not be guaranteed for the relatively long period suggested by the hon. member, or for some other similar period.
In respect to the new procedures for abandonment, I hope it will be agreed that the priority should be given to those lines that carry the least traffic, unless they are situated in an isolated area, are the only form of transport and are required there. But speaking generally, those lines carrying the least traffic will be the ones considered first.
I think that if these procedures are followed, then most of the fears that the hon. gentleman and I well know do exist in western Canada will be removed very quickly. I would be hopeful that something very like the consensus suggested by the hon. gentleman would be reached. I do not expect that we will get everybody to agree; we never can. But I think that we would make very rapid progress in this field; at least, that is my hope. I am very grateful to the hon. gentleman, as I say, who has given a great deal of study to this matter, as we all know, for giving me the opportunity to agree with him.
