The same thing could apply when we come to look at passenger services. We will have to pay subsidies for passenger services which lose money, but which costing figures will we use? The minister says we will use the government's costing figures, but in the past, the government has gone to whom? It has gone, and it goes to the Board of Transport Commissioners. And what figures does the Board of Transport Commissioners use? It uses the railway's figures; so that you might as well not bother with that procedure. I am simply saying that we have a responsibility in this legislation to give some sort of directive to the transport commission which would indicate some guide lines for them to follow in deciding which costing procedure we will start with. We ought to be laying down the procedure, which they can change as they learn more from year to year. As the board gets more and more staff members, who are experts in this business, it will be able to compete with the railway economists and with the railway accountants. There may be better ideas from other quarters of the house, but I do think that on the question of costing and costing procedures the new board will have to be directed for a few years yet by parliament.
I want to add one more point to what I have said about costing. Two years ago I suggested that we should look at each of our areas in western Canada, by areas. Now I think we should make it clear in this legislation that we are going to look at the prairies as a unit, and that the railways will have to prove loss on the prairies rather than on individual lines from point A to B. All the way through this bill you see this business of costing your losses on the basis of having a starting place and a finishing place on a line. This is what sends us up the wall. At the very beginning of section 314, dealing with the matter of lines, it refers to-
-the costs incurred by the company in any financial year thereof in the operation of the line and in the movement of traffic originating or terminating on the line,
And it goes on to say: over
(ii) the revenues of the company for that year from the operation of the line and from the movement of traffic originating or terminating on the line:
This business of determining that the loss will be the loss from point A to point B means that the taxpayer is helpless, because we have no way of ascertaining for sure what 
the costs and revenues with respect to that line are, except by accepting the railway's figures. Therefore, to get away from this trap that is in the legislation, when considering these lines that are up for possible abandonment I think we should look at the whole thing on an area basis, and the area should be the whole region. It must be remembered that these lines that are above the marginal level in their generation of grain shipments add to the profit of other sections of the line. It is when we forget this, that we could fall into a trap, as legislators, if we accept this definition of costing in the bill. When we use figures with respect of point A and point B, what do we know? What are the real losses? We are in a complete trap and at the mercy of the railway accountant.

speechtext: That applies also to the costs of operating.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
That is what I said. We can look at the revenue figures, but unless we have some way of costing, we are completely helpless. Therefore, adopting this principle in the bill of taking point A to point B, in my opinion at least, is bad. We cannot allow the taxpayers to be robbed, on a principle such as this. The only fair way to do it is to put the whole area together.
We will co-operate in getting rid of lines which are not necessary. Fortunately, there are not too many of these now. But when the matter is all rationalized, and operating, we will not give the railways a single cent until they do the things we want. In other words, there is no subsidy and no help until they rationalize their operations in all these areas, as the government directs them to. And if this rationalization procedure is not acceptable to the railways, there are no subsidies, period. That is the only language they will understand, and that is the only way to get these things done.
When I see a section such as the one I have referred to, I have to warn the house and I have to warn the country that we are turning ourselves-that is the taxpayers of this country-over to the hands of the railway accountant. This we cannot allow.
The next subject has to do with the super board. We have had three boards before, handling aeronautics, rail and water. Now we have a board that handles rail, air, water, motor transport-I suppose that includes buses as well as trucks-commodity pipe lines, and other things. Bridges do not come under the board, but are administered by the Department of Public Works. The theory is
September 2, 1966

that by having one board, or with supervision at the top over the five sections of it, we will be able to co-ordinate things better. This theory sounds good, but all sorts of questions come into my mind.
In the past all these boards have tended to operate purely on precedent. The precedents of one board however, are isolated from the precedents of other boards. In the period in between, when there will be this adjustment to a super board, I presume the tendency will be for the board to accept the precedents from the original three boards. To my mind this might be a good opportunity to hear from various hon. members of this house as to how they feel, or as to how parliament feels about laying down some guide lines and some terms of reference, so that this super board will know what we feel about certain things.
Let us take an example. Over and over again in this bill is repeated the fact that every rail rate charged to the shipper shall be compensatory. The bill says that the railways cannot charge a rate which is less than the variable cost. This is an out-of-pocket affair. We will not let the railways charge less than it costs to transport certain goods. That sort of provision is primarily put in as a protection to truckers. But now that we are going to take over interprovincial trucking we will have to deal with the truckers to work out some of the arrangements for their freight rates. What is the attitude of the house about setting rates which are below trucking costs? What control can the board have over this when, at the present time, this is up to the provinces.
I think this is a question that should be looked into. If the interprovincial truckers come under federal legislation, and if we are going to turn over to this super board, the power of running this whole country, this is the time when parliament should lay down the terms, limits or directions for this board to adopt. I should put this in the form of a question, because quite frankly I have not come to any conclusion of what we can do on that score.
But I do say that if we are going to force the railways not to go below a certain price or charge, and if we are going to take over air transportation and trucks, we should be careful in co-ordinating tariff rates.
The next question, that of passenger services, is a subject on which many hon. members will have much to say, and many ideas to express. Under the proposals in this bill
Transportation
the railways are going to be allowed to abandon passenger services on the basis of cost, and if we as a parliament or government decide that they must continue passenger services for the national interest, then we are going to pay 80 per cent of the losses.
The first question I ask is, who is going to do the costing on that? But beyond that there is a bigger question. Today the C.N.R. railway management holds to the view that there is a future in passenger services in Canada, and is doing all it can to get passengers to ride the C.N.R. When passengers get on C.N.R. trains the management does everything it can through its staff to make travel as comfortable and friendly as possible. Here you have a railway management and staff all pulling together to get people to ride on their railway. But when you go from the C.N.R. to the C.P.R. it is just like going from a nice warm pleasant bath to a cold frigid shower, because apparently at the top level of the C.P.R. they have decided that they do not want passenger service, and by various means they have got this philosophy through to some members of their staff, with the result that the most frightful things happen to you on the C.P.R.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
You can phone up for a reservation and they say, "Oh, we cannot get you a reservation for days, weeks or months." The first two or three times you get fooled by this, but then you walk down to the station, walk on to a train and take a chance that you can con the sleeping car conductor into getting you some accommodation. Then finally, when you get into the sleeping car you find it is half empty.
When you say to the conductor, "There is something funny going on; I have tried for days to get a reservation," he usually replies, "I don't know anything about that. All I know is, there's a lot of space here." On three occasions this last summer I was unable to get space on a C.P.R. train, but I took a chance, walked on, and every time I found any accommodation I wanted.

I think my point is well made. I believe it should be pointed out to

September 2, 1966
Transportation
the C.P.R. that if they want to abandon all their passenger services, we realize we cannot force a railway company to haul passengers. We cannot force them to be nice to their customers if they do not want customers, but we do have a right to say that we want running rights over the C.P.R. lines so that the C.N.R. can carry passengers and give somebody some service.
While speaking on this question of passenger service I must say that I have seen morale decline among C.P.R. employees. I have seen morale decline on the express services. I cannot understand, and neither can the railway workers understand what management is trying to do. Here is a railway company that over the years has served Canada tremendously.
Coming from a C.P.R. family myself I know of days when the C.P.R. was tough and hard, and the employees were proud, as rail-waymen, to work for a tough and hard company. If a man made a mistake he got some black marks, some demerit marks; but the men did their best to get the odd merit mark. They were proud of a railway that was rated as a crackerjack railway. But now when you talk to railwaymen on the C.P.R. they do not know how to explain this new management attitude.
This is a problem that affects the efficiency of the company and we have a right to bring it to the attention of the C.P.R. If they want to get out of passenger services they should do it in an honourable and open way, and let arrangements be made for the other fine to carry passengers over their rails. These are questions which other hon. members will raise in this debate.
Turning to the question of commodity pipe lines, to my knowledge Canada at the present time has not got a single commodity pipe fine. Oil and gas are covered under the national energy legislation, but apparently the government proposes to bring this new type of operation under the transportation board. I think the logic is good.
When you look at the bill you see the government has included some sections of the National Energy Board Act, to protect Canadian ownership and management, and I suspect this is the only place in the bill where it is proposed to give power to the government to direct. It does not direct the railways, trucks and air lines, but people engaging in commodity pipe fines are going to be

directed by the government. I think the reason the cabinet's courage got so high is that there is at present nobody to direct.
Are we just to set up a framework of technical regulations? What are the terms of reference under which we want this section of the board to operate? For example, how are charges going to be set on commodity pipe lines? Whether you like it or not, Mr. Speaker, a pipe line is a type of monopoly, and a type of monopoly must have some control over charges.
Are we going to use the principle laid down and accepted in the oil and gas industry, namely that the charge must be such that the maximum return on capital is 7J per cent. Are we going to allow this 7J per cent based on a rate base system, a combination of equity and bonding debentures? What are the terms? I ask, has not parliament the duty to see that something is done in this respect, that something is laid down much more clearly respecting the guiding of these commodity pipe fines for the protection of the public, and so that the companies can operate efficiently and rationally?
I said last night that as a person who is very friendly to the concept of railways I have long hoped for the day when railways would go into all types of transportation, such as air and water. Now pipe lines are going to become a bigger and bigger part of the transportation picture and the railways, in order to keep themselves fully competitive and integrated, should be one of the first types of companies to move into commodity pipe fines.
If more and more of the goods of the country are going to be hauled by pipe lines, then the railways should be planning now to set up pipe fine companies either as subsidiaries or separate entities. Sometimes I think it would be best for the two companies to work together, although this creates a monopoly. If they do not get into this field, transportation revenues will pass away to competitors and once again the industry will go into a decline.
We have all heard about the studies presently being conducted into the movement of grain through a commodity pipe line. Other hon. members are more knowledgeable than I with respect to the technical terms, such as the slurry technique and the capsule technique, but certainly within the next decade grain, potash and wood chips, which were once heavy bulk products handled by railways, will be handled by pipe fines.
September 2, 1966

The contention that I am putting forward now is really none of my business. I cannot force the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. to go into the pipe line business, but I think we should let those companies know we in this house feel that they should be looking to this new form of transportation in order to keep themselves alive and competitive. I would even go so far as to suggest they should consider not only commodities carried by pipe line, within the definition of this bill, but also the question of oil, which we shall have to consider within the next few years.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
There is another point in this bill about which I am very worried. In the old bill we had clauses on agreed charges; now they are out. This is another reason I was completely pessimistic as I read the bill. The agreed charge section is out. What is the agreed charge section? This is a section which allows the railways, when building a market, to charge a rate which is not compensatory, because they know that at the end of three, four, five or six years the market will develop to such a point that they will be in the black. You cannot develop a country, particularly in the mining and wooded areas, unless in the first stage there is a loss period.
The railways now are forbidden to open up a new area like this, if this section is out. I may be wrong, but as I read this section it seems to me it has disappeared. I can refer to it at page 49. I see the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Turner) shakes his head. It says:
The heading preceding section 349 and section 349 of the said Act are repealed.
The note says:
This section permits the board to authorize special rates for specific shipments between points not being competitive points, to develop trade or to create business, or for the advantage of the public interest, if not otherwise contrary to the act.
As the clause says, it is going to be repealed; and as the explanation of the clause stands, I can only take it that the section is out. The agreed rate system can be helpful; only if it is hurting anybody else in opening up an area is it not helpful. We know that the minimum rates are compensatory; it is repeated again and again in the act. It is for the protection of the trucking industry. The maximum rate control provisions in this bill are the same as they were in 1964. The clauses in respect of the captive shipper are lengthy. Many people think they are adequate, but frankly I know that some will
Transportation
debate the details of the captive shipment
principles. I will leave that to the experts.
What I should like to wind up with, and express in the strongest terms, is that under this bill I do not see an end to the discrimination in rates. In looking at page 51 of the bill under the part headed "traffic, tolls and tariffs", I find that it reads as follows:
381. (1) All tolls shall be just and reasonable, and shall always, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions with respect to all traffic of the same description carried over the same route, be charged equally to all persons at the same rate.
That sounds wonderful, but there is one thing left out. What about region to region? This is where I need the help of persons who are extremely qualified in interpreting this. To me this reads that, in respect of an article going over the same route, any person buying a similar article in the same area gets the same rate. Suppose I live in Saskatchewan, that this rate applies only from Toronto to Sudbury and I want to get the same type of goods from Winnipeg to Saskatchewan. All the people in that area get the same deal under this section, but it may be anything at all compared to the rate from Toronto to Sudbury or vice-versa. The way this is written I do not see anything but regional discrimination again.
What has been the policy all down through the years? This is what the fight has been about. As the railways needed more money, from the thirties on, they applied freight rate increases all across the board-10 per cent, 12 per cent, 17 per cent. They obtained authority from the Board of Transport Commissioners to apply this all across Canada, but they never applied it all across the country. They applied it only in the areas where there is no competition. In the main, these areas were the maritimes and the prairies. The same discrimination applied in areas of northern Ontario and northern Quebec, but the only thing different about the northern areas of Quebec and Ontario in relation to the maritimes and the prairies is that no one in these areas has fought for these people; that is the reason they never heard much about it. This discrimination, however, has been consistent. Every time the railways wanted more money, up went the rates. Naturally we look for a clear explanation. Goods of the same sort carried the same distance should be shipped for the same price whether in Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Ontario or British Columbia. That should be the principle; we have fought so hard to get this principle accepted.

September 2, 1966
Transportation
I am only a layman and others may have an interpretation which will clear this up, but unless I am misreading the bill, this principle is not contained in it. I have to tell the minister that in spite of his remarks this morning I cannot vote for the second reading of this bill until this point is cleared up. This is the reason that yesterday I made the appeal that we do not have this debate on second reading. I do not want to stop the good sections of this bill because of the things with which I do not agree; but this is all fundamental to our economic well-being. I do not wish to turn over to the railways the right to say that one area will develop and another will stagnate. Being extreme in my views, it seems that a railway could decide to ship goods from Winnipeg to Brandon at such and such a rate, and at a different rate from Winnipeg to Kenora. One town would have high rates and all the people in that area would have high rates, while all the people in the other area would have low rates. I have spoken to a good many people who feel as I do, and this is the interpretation they put on it. This is the reason I have no choice but to fight as hard as I can and as long as I can. This is a battle we have had for 30 years and it must be cleared up in a manner satisfactory to all.
I appeal to all parties in this house, not only on the opposite side, to realize that this is the key, the real issue. We can resolve the question of railway line abandonments in western Canada. But the point on which the country is dependent is that there will be equality in carrying a certain amount of goods a certain distance and that the rate should be the same in any part of the country. That is the main contention that I put forward. I am not going to deal with the matter of the maritime freight rates or the grain rates; they are protected for two or three years.

are a great many details with which we are not familiar. We did not have the opportunity of questioning the minister to obtain clarification of a great many points. Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. gentleman is not attempting to misrepresent what I said. I said exactly what he is now saying. There are two kinds of politics. One is the kind that all of us who have any self-respect in this house are proud to practice, while the other is the kind which editorial writers seem to have on the brain and which I would describe as a dubious kind of conduct which is not confined by any means to politics.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I was about to say that part of the sorry mess transportation is in at this time has been in large part due to the shenanigans that have gone on among railway promoters and politicians. In that regard, as I shall show later on in my remarks, I think the sooner we get politics out of transportation the better it will be for Canada. When the minister says that we must have politics in transportation I take it he means we cannot have transportation in this country without government control and direction. I am completely in agreement with that suggestion. One cannot operate a transportation system in the same way as one operates a soap factory or an automobile assembly line. A transportation system cannot be operated merely on a profit and loss statement. A transportation system, particularly in Canada, has certa'n very definite functions to perform. As the minister said last night, transportation has been the life line of Canada. Here we are, 20 million people spread across the American border stretching for some 4,000 miles, with a depth varying from 200 to 300 miles in the settled parts of our population. We have a straggling, sparsely settled population that must be linked by adequate transportation

Transportation
services. From the time Canada was born transportation has been the main consideration of the governments that brought Canada into existence and have conducted its affairs in all the years from then until now.
There are few countries in the world that are so dependent upon transportation. We are dependent upon transportation because such a large part of our produce has to find its way into world markets. There are few countries in the world where the people spend such a high proportion of their per capita income on the transportation of goods and people. Consequently for nearly 100 years transportation has been a matter of national policy and could not be conducted in the way one would conduct an ordinary business of manufacturing or mining.
One of the principles that has had to be followed is that a transportation system must get our primary goods, as well as our manufactured goods, to world markets at competitive prices. This is why we have had such things as the Crowsnest pass agreement, to allow the farmers of the prairies to get their grain into world markets. This is why we have had various subsidies to enable Canadian manufacturers and primary producers of minerals, pulp and timber to get their goods into world markets.
In addition to that, national policy has dictated that Canada had to develop its great industrial potential in central Canada. This is a fact that is sometims forgotten. We often meet people who tell us how much assistance has been given to the people of the maritimes and the people on the praries in the way of various subventions, subsidies or fixed shipping rates. But it is equally true that part of our national policy has been directed toward bringing raw materials to the great industrial complex of central Canada as cheaply as possible, and to bring fuel to central Canada. That is why we have had subventions on coal from the maritimes into central Canada. It has not been merely to enable the maritimes to sell coal but to given central Canada cheap fuel. That is why we have given assistance in putting gas pipe lines through to central Canada. That is why we have special rates on shipping feed grain from western to central Canada, to enable the farmers of central Canada to fatten their cattle for market.
I am not complaining about it, but I am simply pointing out that part of the national policy for decades has not only been to allow primary producers to get their products into world markets at competitive prices but also

September 2, 1966
to help central Canada by giving them raw material's, feed grain and fuel at the lowest possible cost. The result of this, of course, has been to produce a freight rate structure that is a veritable nightmare. I had the privilege on two or three occasions of appearing, along with the late Hon. Angus Macdonald, the former premier of Nova Scotia, and the late Hon. J. L. Kalston, before the federal cabinet to appeal freight rate decisions of the Board of Transport Commissioners.
I think anyone who has tried to study the freight rate structure will agree that the longer you study it, the less you know about it. The freight rate structure is like the peace of the Lord; it passeth all understanding. But the fact is, of course, that we have learned to live with it. I think it can be improved. I think the discriminatory features need to be removed. I believe we should look very carefully at this bill which, while it may take some of the anomalies out of the freight rate structure, introduces an entirely new principle which could be dangerous in the extreme; because as I see this legislation it is designed to let competition solve our major problems in transportation. It is designed on the thesis that the competitive forces of the alternative modes of transportation will be effective in preventing exploitation of the shipper, and any abuse on the part of those who are in the transportation business. This was stated very clearly by the minister last night at page 7991 of Hansard when he said, referring to the MacPherson report:
But the basic approach of the report was a new one. It was that there has been a development of alternative and competitive modes of transport in most parts of the country for most classes of travel, and that the kind of regulation of railway charges and practices by a regulatory body which may have been needed in the past was no longer essential for the protection of the public.
Mr. Speaker, that is a very debatable contention. I am afraid that in making that statement the minister let his free enterprise bias influence his judgment.

I have no objection at all. As
a matter of fact I was going to deal with these very points and will do so if the minister would just possess his soul in patience.
I want to ask in the first place: Where will this genuine competition exist? What are the alternative modes of transportation that will provide the competition so as to keep rates at a reasonable level? The argument is immediately put forth that the trucking industry will provide this kind of competition in some parts of Canada. And yet the fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that both the large railways in Canada have been acquiring large trucking operations, that they are already operating interprovincial trucking firms in this country, and that many of the trucking companies in Canada are just waiting to get a lucrative offer from either of the railroads. As the railways move into the trucking business- and I do not blame them for doing so; they would be very foolish to stay with only one form of transportation-which they have done and will do in increasing measure, where will the competition be then? Will the shipper have the choice between shipping by the railways or shipping by trucks owned by the railways, or maybe eventually by pipe line owned by the railways? We will be leaning on a broken reed if we depend on competition to keep transportation rates at a price that is fair and reasonable to the shippers who want to get their goods to market at competitive prices.

September 2, 1966
Transportation
Second, what about the areas where there are no alternative forms of transportation? The areas in the maritimes, in northern Quebec, northern Ontario and on the prairies will not have alternate modes, and large parts of these regions cannot have a trucking service that is independent from the railroad. These regions will not have the kind of competition which would keep rates at a reasonable figure. What alternative will the shipper on the prairies have, one who wants to ship livestock over long distances, or the potash and the mining companies? What about the lumber companies and the pulp and paper companies of northern Ontario and Quebec?
The maritimes will have some protection for two years, but they too have always faced this serious situation, which we also have in western Canada, that whenever the railway companies have been given permission to raise the rates it has been the Atlantic provinces and western Canada which have borne the brunt of those rate increases. I cannot see anything in this bill that will give any guarantee of protection to the shippers of these areas.
If the government is going to take the
wraps off the railroads, it will be able to get more money, which it claims it needs. I have very strong fears that the areas from which they are going to get that extra money are western Canada, northern Ontario and Quebec, and probably later on the maritime provinces.
In the television address which the Prime Minister delivered over the national hook-up on August 23 of this year he said this to the
Canadian people:
Necessary increases in wages oi the railway workers since 1960 have on three separate occasions, been met by government subsidies to the railways. Such subsidies are now costing the taxpayers of Canada $100 million a year. The government cannot continue to provide subsidies to pay railway workers without imposing higher taxes. This we are not prepared to ask parliament to do.
We do, however, intend to ask parliament immediately to pass transportation legislation based broadly on recommendations of the royal commission on transportation. This legislation will give the railways greater freedom to adjust their charges to meet competition and increase their earnings. Therefore, it should enable the railways themselves to bear the burden of a legitimate increase in wages.
This legislation, as hon. members know, called for the steady reduction of that $100 million annual subsidy over a period of eight years.

Where will the railways get this extra money to reimburse them for the loss of a $100 million subsidy and to enable them to pay increased wages? We may speculate on whether or not it is fair to have a subsidy which is paid for by all the people of Canada or else say to the railways: You can get this money instead out of levying higher freight rates on those areas of Canada where the competition places you in a position of monopoly.
[DOT] {4:40 p.m.)
I greatly fear that the removal of restraints and restrictions on railways with reference to freight rates will mean that certain regions of Canada, those I have already named, are going to pay the shot and that some of the burden which heretofore had been borne by all the people of Canada is going to fall upon those areas of Canada which can least afford to carry this burden. Certainly the maritime provinces cannot afford to carry it. They will have a couple of years of grace, but we do not know what will happen after that. Certainly the northern part of Ontario and Quebec cannot carry it. Already the prairie provinces are paying freight rates that are much higher than those paid in other parts of Canada, and they should not be called upon to carry this extra burden. If there had to be extra money for the railways, surely that is a matter of national policy. The funds to provide that extra revenue ought to be provided equitably by all parts of Canada and not the parts of Canada that at the present time are less prosperous and have less industrial development than other parts of this country.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe that free enterprise and the competitive system of transportation can give Canada an adequate transportation policy at a price we can afford. There may be countries where they can afford to have all sorts of free enterprise and competition; different forms of transportation and different companies competing with each other, duplicating services. However, in a country of 20 million people where, as I said before, we are more dependent than probably any country in the world on getting our goods to market over long distances at competitive prices, where we spend more per capita on transportation than probably any other country in the world, I do not think we can afford the luxury of having a free enterprise, competitive transportation policy.

task of getting people and goods from point A to point B, and the best way to get them from the one point to the other. We should have thought of integrating all forms of transportation so that one form of transportation would complement the other rather than duplicating it.
Every hon. member who has travelled across Canada knows that railway lines sometimes run close enough together that one could throw a baseball from one set of lines to the other. There is endless duplication. I can take members to places where two sets of transcontinental lines and the trans-Canada highway all run within sight of each other, and all are used as a means of hauling similar goods. There has been no co-ordination and no integration because we have thought in terms of separate modes of transportation rather than in terms of a single transportation system that would move goods and people from one point to another.
What I should like to see in this legislation is not just a commission set up, but a Canadian transportation authority clothed with the power to begin to integrate and to co-ordinate all forms of national transportation in Canada, so that we will be able to eliminate the wastefulness, duplication and overlapping which we cannot afford in a country like Canada, if we are to convey our goods to world markets at competitive prices without having to subsidize their carriage out of the public treasury.
I think this probably means that such a transportation authority would have to begin with the integration of the two railway systems. Instead of having some of the ridiculous anomalies which were pointed out by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), and which I need not repeat, such as going 100 miles north and then 100 miles south again rather than switching on to the other company's line, examples such as this which can be duplicated at various points across Canada should be eliminated. It does not make sense not to have these railway systems integrated, certainly as far as passenger traffic and freight are concerned.
I think that the day will undoubtedly come when these two railways will have to be integrated as part of a government transportation system. By that time the railways themselves will probably be operating a good part of the interprovincial trucking system.
I think that a national transportation authority will have to move into the field of pipe lines for moving solids. Because if it
tMr. Douglas.]
does not, and if the public transportation system is to operate railroads and allow some free enterprise promoters to operate pipe lines, we will be back to the old situation of the government owning the most costly form of transportation and allowing private enterprise to make a lot of money out of other forms of transportation.
I am not hopeful that the government is going to be sufficiently farsighted that it is going to move as fast as I would like it to move. I want to tell the government that if it does not do this the day is coming when some government and some parliament will, in the not too distant future, be compelled by the pressure of economic events to take all of our national transportation systems and weld them into a single public utility. I think that is inevitable, and it would be far better if this were done right away.

One good thing about the minister's bill is that it does propose to set up this Canadian Transport Commission which, while it has no power, has some regulatory authority and will do considerable research into the various forms of transportation. It is a first faltering step, and it will at least provide the framework within which this government or some other government, if it has the courage, will be able to build a genuine national transportation authority and eventually to establish national transportation as a public utility.
Therefore, I hope that this first faltering step which the government is taking will be followed up very quickly. I am convinced that this government or the government that succeeds it will find that in a few years this transport commission, because of its lack of power and authority, will not be able to solve
September 2, 1966

the problem. If the house does not at this time give that commission some power and put some teeth into the bill, then some subsequent parliament will be compelled to do so, after we have lost valuable years and very large sums of money.
In his speech on September 14, 1964, the minister said that this legislation was revolutionary. Well, we have heard of the quiet revolution, and we now have what I would call the timid revolution. It is a very tepid revolution. It is a move in the right direction and will bring the various forms of transportation at least under regulation. It is a start. But I hope that before the committee to which this bill is being referred reports back, it will give very serious consideration to putting some real muscle into this act so that the Canadian Transport Commission will become an authority, not merely a regulatory body.
I would urge the committee of the house to which this bill will be referred to think of transportation for Canada in terms of the last quarter of the twentieth century and the first quarter of the twenty-first century, rather than in terms of the nineteenth century. If transportation was vital to the economic life of Canada 100 years ago when the fathers of confederation began to dream of binding Canada from sea to sea with a ribbon of steel, how much more vital is it today in a world that is shrinking so rapidly, a world where it is absolutely essential to move goods cheaply and quickly if we are to retain our place as one of the great trading nations of the world.
The minister is right when he says that transportation is Canada's life line. If that transportation system is not efficient, if it does not provide service as cheaply as possible, if it does not free itself from wasteful duplication, then this country will suffer the economic consequences of our neglect and of our lack of vision.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that when this legislation goes to the committee of the house it will get a full and complete revision, not in the light of past experience alone, but in the light of the great changes which face Canada in the future.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset, when the Minister of Transport was introducing this bill into the house, he made some point about politics in
Transportation
transportation. I think he went on to define the different meanings in the word "politics".
First, I should say that I appreciate the interpretation or connotation that the Minister of Transport put on the word "politics", and with the connotation that he used with respect to politics in transportation I agree. In spite of all attempts by editorial writers, and so on, across the country during the past two or three years in particular to degrade politics and politicians generally, we still must recognize that it is the politicians, particularly in this house, who stand between the government and the governed. That essentially is a noble function. It is also true that those politicians who have been maligned and degraded stand between the monopolistic interests in the country and the people of the country. Here again they perform a noble purpose. This purpose I think is being served reasonably well by politicians.
The Minister of Transport also commended to the members of this house the first clause of the bill defining a national transportation policy, and asked us to read it. I have read it. While it is very short, certainly no one can disagree with the objectives outlined in that brief statement.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, we go on to read the rest of the bill, and we find outlined in the balance of the bill the ways and means of achieving the objectives that have been outlined in the statement of policy. I do not think the Minister of Transport would be critical if I suggested that there could be wide disagreement on the ways and means of giving effect to these objectives, so far as the other clauses are concerned.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, as I look over the bill, those remarks might apply so far as the new transport commission is concerned. I agree with some of the other statements which have been made, that it is a step in the right direction. Although I will not cite cases today, the very fact of air routes and railway lines having been referred to different boards has had the end result of denying certain communities in Canada adequate transportation from either the one form of transport or the other. I hope that there will be an improvement in co-ordination so far as the public interest is concerned, when the new transport commission is set up, and I hope that the board will consider all modes of transport, so far as the over-all requirements of each community are concerned.

September 2, 1966
Transportation
We have to examine in great detail the powers and duties of this new transport commission. As I look over some clauses of the bill I find that there are differences between
powers that appear to be assigned to this commission and the powers that the existing
Board of Transport Commissioners has had in the past. I am not going into detail, but I
should like to quote one example. We have had what might be termed a long standing
traditional right that any shipper could go before the Board of Transport Commissioners
and plead discrimination-discrimination in his own individual case, so far as rates are concerned, and as those rates applied to his own personal or corporate business. That provision was contained in section 317, I believe, of the old Railway Act. The provisions appearing in the new bill, defining the powers and duties of the new Canadian Transport Commission, are such that an individual shipper will have to prove, before his case can be valid, that the discriminatory rates he is charged, if you want to call them that, affect the public interest. I hope this will not be the case, because, surely, some small corporation or individual should not have to go before the transport commission and prove that the public interest is being damaged because of a rate being charged to him. Yet that is what the new act seems to provide.
The long standing tradition to which I have referred is something that shippers have valued and used for many, many years; namely the privilege of being able to go before the Board of Transport Commissioners and prove that there was discrimination against them in relation to other shippers of a similar kind, with the result that a railway company could be ordered to change its rates and remove the discrimination. That sort of thing appears to have gone, as I read this bill.
Talking in the same vein, in the bill before us there is no definition of the words "public interest". During the course of his political career I know the minister has probably used the words "public interest" thousands of times. I have used them, and I expect every hon. member of the house has used them. But what do they mean, so far as railway rates are concerned? They are not defined in the bill. Do they mean that an individual shipper who ships, say, for 500 miles or for smaller distances from his point of origin must prove that something affecting him has to do with the public interest, affecting the people from

Bonavista to Vancouver Island? That is an
unreasonable condition. The reason I raise the point now is that we are discussing the principle of a new railway act. That long standing tradition that a shipper might apply to the board, pleading discrimination so far as rates are concerned, has not been incorporated in this bill. I hope the minister will correct this deficiency, and perhaps something can be done by way of suggestion or amendment in committee which the minister will be prepared to accept.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I am not going to speak more about the transport commission, except to say I think there is some value in co-ordinating supervision over all the modes of transportation that come under federal jurisdiction, so that there will not be a withdrawal of vital services by one mode, and then by another, leaving communities without adequate service by any mode.
The bill also makes provision to deal with commodity pipe lines. As the minister said, this is something we shall probably have to be concerned with in the future. It is not a major problem at the moment. It is not even a major factor in our economic structure at the moment, but it is probably good to consider it and have something in the statute so that we may have a starting point when problems arise.
Another part of the bill deals with motor transport. It constitutes a very timid move, and this is probably good because for the most part the provincial governments are responsible for motor transport. After all, provincial governments have built most, in fact almost all of the highways, and therefore moving into this field timidly and gently is probably a good thing.
Another provision allows for transfer of responsibility for bridges from the Board of Transport Commissioners to the Department of Public Works. I do not think it is of any particular concern which department handles them, so long as it looks after the public interest.
So far as railway rationalization is concerned, I was pleased to hear the Minister of Transport say that at the outset they are going to establish a minimum grid system of railways in the prairies. The provincial government of Alberta, which has the same political affiliation as my party in the house, has been asking for this for a long time. At this point I do not know whether the grid
September 2, 1966

system to be established will be completely satisfactory to everyone involved. As the minister said, most likely it will not, but at least a start will be made on it.
Before dealing with the rate making provisions, which are probably the most important part of the bill, I wish to deal with the principle which claims that the transport commission ought to have greater power to direct and control all modes of transport, so that over-all transport policy is directed by the commission.
In my opinion it is a fallacy to argue that an appointed board, no matter how competent the appointees may be, is in a better position to direct all transportation policy for Canada than a number of individual groups and companies who are trying to move goods, people and commodities in Canada at the lowest possible cost, in order to do well by their companies. I do not buy the argument that it is better for an over-all authority to give directives and have complete control. Experience has shown that this has not proven to be the case in other areas. Of course, because of the nature of our geography, there are cases of monopolies, and in that instance there is justification for some government control.
The possibility, indeed the probability of change in rate making envisaged by the bill is the most important feature of it. I say that, because on less than 5 per cent of the total commodities and goods now being shipped is the ceiling rate charged.

pound car, you get the cost of moving a

We wish to know in dollars and cents what some of these things will amount to when the calculations are made.
So, Mr. Speaker, I will close now in the hope that this bill will go to the committee. However, before I conclude I should like to suggest to the minister, and to the house particularly, because I know the minister does not have full control of this matter, that while we have perhaps a little more urgent responsibility and a little more pressure upon us, because of things that happened this week and last week, to get a new railway act, that
September 2, 1966
we do not try to rush it through the committee. We would hope that it would get the attention and study which it deserves.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I think it is fair to suggest that it is necessary for all interested parties to have at least a three week period to consider this bill and present a report. It is a long and complex subject. Hon. members should have an opportunity to study it and then collect their thoughts. I know there will be a great deal of pressure to get the committee started. I hope the pressure will not be such that we cannot give this bill the consideration it deserves.
In closing let me make one other point, and I may say that I hesitate to refer to this at this time. I am haunted by a suspicion that this dispute between the railway companies and the railway unions was partly prompt-ed-and that is perhaps a harsh word-by the railway companies in order to put pressure on parliament to pass this bill. During the eight months prior to December, 1965, and even before that, until the strike took place there was really no serious attempt made by the railway companies to negotiate with the unions. The companies made no reasonable offer at all, nor was any indication of any offer made public.
I do not like this kind of pressure put on members of parliament as a result of power politics, if that is what happened, to force us into passing rapidly this new railway act. As I said, I have been haunted by the suspicion that that is what happened, because during the past few months there have been indications that a strike was imminent. Everyone apparently knew that a strike would take place; yet during that time the railway companies claimed their hands were tied until the government passed legislation necessary to allow them to increase revenues in order to meet the union demands. The companies complained about competition and the inability to compete, using this as a reason for not being able to meet demands for higher wages.
Transportation If competition has prevented them from making bigger profits in order to pay higher wages, that is one thing; but the companies should not blame the government or parliament for not moving to free them from an unfair position.
I do not intend to say anything more at the moment. I am sure we will have a very useful and constructive discussion at committee meetings. We in this party have a number of suggestions to make and I hope the minister will accept them as constructive suggestions which may improve the ways and means of giving effect to a good national transportation policy, which we agree must be established at this time.
